The Online Web-Based Training and Certification System is a web-based application developed to improve the delivery of online education and professional training. The system allows students to access training resources from any location using a web browser, eliminating the limitations of traditional classroom-based learning.

Students can create accounts, log in securely, browse available courses, enroll in training programs, access videos and study materials, attempt certification examinations, and instantly receive downloadable digital certificates upon successful completion of the course.

The administrator manages all system activities through a secure dashboard. Administrative responsibilities include creating and publishing courses, uploading learning resources, configuring quizzes, managing student records, generating reports, and maintaining system security.

The system automatically evaluates certification examinations, calculates scores, determines pass or fail status, and generates PDF certificates for successful students. This automation reduces manual work, improves efficiency, and provides a reliable method for tracking student progress and certification records.

Safety requirements for the Online Web-Based Training and Certification System (OWTCS) ensure that the platform behaves predictably, protects learners and administrators from harmful outcomes, and does not become a source of data corruption, service failure, or misuse. Unlike purely functional requirements, safety requirements describe how the system must prevent, detect, and recover from conditions that could cause harm to users, data, or the organization operating the platform. The following sub-sections describe the core safety obligations of the system.
Input Validation and Prevention of Harmful Actions

Every field in the system — learner registration forms, course enrollment forms, quiz and assessment submissions, certificate requests, and instructor content uploads — must be validated both on the client side (for immediate feedback) and on the server side (for enforcement), since client-side checks can be bypassed. Validation must reject malformed email addresses, out-of-range dates (such as a certificate expiry date earlier than its issue date), negative or zero values in fields like course duration or passing marks, and file uploads that exceed permitted size or type (only PDF, DOCX, MP4, and image formats should be accepted for course material and profile pictures, with a strict maximum file size).

The system must actively prevent harmful actions such as bulk deletion of learner records without a two-step confirmation, irreversible destructive operations (like deleting a certification exam that already has submitted results) without an administrator override and audit trail, and submission of assessment answers after the allotted time has expired. Rate limiting must be applied to login attempts, quiz submissions, and certificate download requests to prevent automated abuse. Any attempt to inject script tags, SQL fragments, or command sequences into text fields must be sanitized or rejected outright, and the attempt should be logged for security review.

The system must enforce role-based access so that learners, instructors, and administrators can only perform actions appropriate to their role. A learner must never be able to alter their own quiz scores, edit the content of a course, or issue a certificate to themselves. An instructor must be restricted to managing the courses and assessments assigned to them, and must not be able to view or modify another instructor's gradebook without administrative permission. Administrators are the only role permitted to configure system-wide settings, approve certificate templates, or override an automatically generated result.

Every access-controlled action must be checked at the server, not only hidden in the user interface, because hiding a button from a learner does not prevent a technically capable user from calling the underlying function directly. Session tokens must expire after a period of inactivity, and privilege escalation — for example, a learner attempting to reach an administrator-only URL — must return an authorization failure and generate a security log entry rather than exposing any part of the restricted page.

Because the OWTCS stores personal information (names, contact details, educational history, payment records, and government-issued identification numbers used for certificate verification), the system must comply with applicable data protection regulations, including Pakistan's Personal Data Protection framework and, where the platform serves international learners, general principles found in regulations such as the GDPR. This includes obtaining explicit consent before collecting personal data, allowing learners to request a copy of their stored data, and allowing account deletion requests to be honored within a defined timeframe.

The system must also comply with accessibility guidelines (such as WCAG 2.1 Level AA) so that learners with visual, auditory, or motor impairments can use the training portal, and with financial regulations relevant to processing course fees, including secure handling of payment card information in line with PCI-DSS principles if online payment is supported. Certification content must respect intellectual property law, ensuring that course materials uploaded by instructors do not infringe on copyrighted third-party content, and the platform must retain records long enough to satisfy any applicable academic or corporate audit requirements.

Security requirements define the mechanisms the Online Web-Based Training and Certification System must implement to protect the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of learner data, course content, assessment results, and certification records. Because certificates issued by the system may be relied upon by employers or institutions, the integrity and authenticity of stored data is a critical concern that runs through every sub-section below.

All users — learners, instructors, and administrators — must authenticate using a unique username or email combined with a password before accessing any part of the system beyond the public course catalog. Passwords must meet a minimum complexity standard (at least eight characters, including a mixture of upper-case, lower-case, numeric, and special characters) and must never be stored in plain text; the system must use a strong one-way hashing algorithm such as bcrypt or Argon2 with per-user salting. Multi-factor authentication should be available, and mandatory, for administrator accounts, given the sensitivity of the actions they can perform. Failed login attempts must be limited (for example, locking an account for a cooldown period after five consecutive failures) to resist brute-force attacks, and password reset must occur through a time-limited, single-use link sent to a verified email address rather than through a security question alone.

All data transmitted between the learner's browser and the server must be encrypted using TLS 1.2 or higher, so that credentials, quiz answers, and personal information cannot be intercepted on the network. Sensitive data at rest — including password hashes, national identity numbers used for certificate verification, and payment details — must be encrypted in the database using industry-standard algorithms such as AES-256. Encryption keys must be stored separately from the encrypted data, ideally in a dedicated key-management service, and must be rotated periodically according to a documented schedule to limit the impact of any single key compromise.

Beyond basic authentication, the system must implement fine-grained, role-based access control (RBAC) so that every API endpoint and every page verifies the acting user's role and ownership of the resource being requested before returning data. For instance, an instructor requesting a learner's transcript must only succeed if that learner is enrolled in a course the instructor teaches. Access control lists must be centrally defined and enforced through a single authorization layer rather than scattered checks throughout the codebase, so that new features automatically inherit the correct restrictions and audits of the permission model remain straightforward.

The system must maintain a tamper-evident audit log recording who performed which action, on which record, and at what time — covering events such as login attempts (successful and failed), certificate issuance, grade changes, course content edits, and

administrative configuration changes. Logs must be retained for a minimum period consistent with academic and legal record-keeping requirements and must be protected from modification or deletion by the same accounts whose actions they record. Automated monitoring should flag anomalous patterns, such as a sudden spike in certificate downloads from a single account or repeated failed access attempts to administrator pages, and alert system administrators in near real time.

User sessions must be identified using secure, randomly generated tokens that are transmitted only over encrypted connections and marked as HTTP-only and secure cookies to prevent access by client-side scripts. Sessions must automatically expire after a defined period of inactivity (for example, thirty minutes for learners and fifteen minutes for administrators), and users must be able to explicitly log out, which must immediately invalidate the session token on the server rather than relying solely on the client discarding it. Concurrent session limits and re-authentication before high-sensitivity actions, such as changing a password or issuing a certificate manually, add a further layer of protection.

All user-supplied input must be treated as untrusted and validated against a strict allow-list of expected formats before it is processed or stored. The system must use parameterized queries or a vetted object-relational mapper for all database interactions to eliminate SQL injection risk, must encode output correctly to prevent cross-site scripting (XSS) when displaying user-generated content such as discussion forum posts or course reviews, and must implement anti-CSRF tokens on all state-changing forms. File uploads must be scanned and re-validated on the server regardless of client-side restrictions, and executable file types must never be accepted.

Learner data must be collected only for purposes clearly communicated at the point of collection, and access to personally identifiable information must be restricted to the roles that genuinely require it — for example, a course instructor should see a learner's progress and grades but not their payment history. The system should support data minimization by default, anonymizing or aggregating data used for analytics and reporting wherever individual identification is not necessary. Learners must be able to review, correct, and, where legally permitted, request deletion of their personal data through a defined self-service or support process.

Because the OWTCS is expected to be hosted on third-party cloud infrastructure rather than on institution-owned hardware, physical security of the servers, storage, and network equipment is delegated to the hosting provider. The chosen provider must demonstrate compliance with recognized physical security standards, including restricted data-center access, environmental controls, redundant power, and fire suppression systems. The project team remains responsible for verifying the provider's compliance certifications and for configuring the platform's own access controls correctly, since physical security at the data-center level does not substitute for proper application-level security.

Where the system is deployed for institutional or corporate use, the hosting environment and, where feasible, the application itself should aim to align with recognized security frameworks such as ISO/IEC 27001 for information security management and SOC 2 Type II for service organizations. While a student academic project may not pursue formal certification, the design and documentation should demonstrate awareness of these frameworks so the system can be extended toward compliance if it is adopted in a production or commercial context, and periodic security assessments or penetration tests should be planned as the platform matures.

Software quality attributes, also called non-functional requirements, describe the overall characteristics the Online Web-Based Training and Certification System must exhibit beyond its functional features. These attributes determine how well the system performs under real conditions, how easily it can be maintained and extended, and how confidently it can be trusted by learners, instructors, and administrators.

The system must consistently produce correct results across repeated use — a quiz submitted by a learner must always be graded using the same rules, and a certificate generated for a given result must always contain accurate data. The system should be designed to recover gracefully from unexpected failures, such as a dropped database connection during a quiz submission, without losing the learner's progress. Automated backups of the database should run on a regular schedule, and a documented recovery procedure should allow the system to be restored to a recent consistent state after a failure.

The interface must be intuitive enough for learners with varying levels of digital literacy to register, enroll in courses, complete lessons, and take assessments without external assistance. Navigation should follow consistent patterns across pages, error messages should clearly explain what went wrong and how to correct it, and critical actions such as final quiz submission should require a confirmation step. The system should be usable on both desktop and mobile browsers, given that learners may access training material from a range of devices and network conditions.

The codebase must be organized into clearly separated modules — for example, distinct components for user management, course management, assessment, and certification — so that a developer can modify one area without unintended side effects elsewhere. Consistent naming conventions, adequate inline documentation, and adherence to the chosen framework's recommended project structure (such as Django's app-based architecture) reduce the effort required to fix defects or add new features. Automated tests covering core business logic further support maintainability by catching regressions early.

The system must be able to accommodate growth in the number of learners, courses, and concurrent assessment sessions without a proportional degradation in performance. This is particularly important during peak periods, such as when many learners attempt a certification exam within the same time window. The architecture should support horizontal scaling of the web application layer, efficient database indexing on frequently queried fields such as learner ID and course ID, and caching of relatively static content like course catalogs to reduce database load.

The system should be deployable across different hosting environments with minimal modification, achieved by avoiding hard dependencies on a single cloud provider's proprietary services where standard alternatives exist, and by containerizing the application using a tool such as Docker so that the runtime environment can be reproduced consistently across development, testing, and production. Configuration values specific to an environment, such as database credentials or API keys, should be externalized rather than hard-coded, allowing the same codebase to run in multiple contexts.

The system should be able to exchange data with external systems where relevant, such as institutional learning management systems, payment gateways for course fees, and email or SMS services for notifications. This is best achieved through well-documented RESTful APIs using standard data formats such as JSON, and by following common authentication standards such as OAuth 2.0 where third-party integration is required. Certificates issued by the system should also be exportable in standard formats such as PDF, and ideally support verification through a shareable link or QR code that external parties can check.

As a quality attribute, security refers to the system's overall resistance to unauthorized access, data breaches, and misuse, complementing the detailed security requirements described in Section 5.3. From a quality perspective, security must be treated as a design consideration from the earliest stages of development rather than added afterward, meaning that authentication, authorization, and data protection mechanisms should be built into the architecture rather than retrofitted once functional features are complete.

Correctness measures how accurately the system implements its specified requirements — for instance, whether the grading algorithm always awards the exact marks defined in the assessment configuration, and whether a certificate is issued only when a learner has genuinely met the passing criteria. Correctness is validated through a combination of unit testing of individual functions (such as the grade calculation logic), integration testing of complete workflows (such as enrollment through certificate issuance), and manual verification against the documented business rules before each release.

The system should be structured so that its components can be tested independently and automatically. Business logic, such as grade calculation or certificate eligibility checks, should be separated from the user interface so that it can be unit-tested without requiring a browser. The use of a well-defined API layer between the frontend and backend also allows automated end-to-end tests to simulate learner actions such as enrollment, quiz submission, and certificate download, making it possible to detect defects before they reach production.

The system should aim for a high level of uptime, particularly during scheduled examination windows when learners depend on the platform being accessible. A target availability of at least 99 percent during business and examination hours is a reasonable goal for an academic-scale deployment, achieved through reliable hosting, monitoring for outages, and a documented plan for scheduled maintenance that avoids peak usage periods such as certification exam dates known in advance.

Business rules define the operational policies the Online Web-Based Training and Certification System must enforce so that training delivery, assessment, certification, and administration remain consistent, fair, and auditable. Unlike technical requirements, business rules originate from how the organization running the platform expects training and certification to be conducted, and the system must encode these rules so they are applied uniformly rather than left to manual judgment.
A learner may enroll in a course only if the course is currently marked as active and open for enrollment, and if any stated prerequisite courses have already been completed and passed.

Each course must define a maximum number of seats where relevant (for instructor-led sessions), and enrollment must be automatically closed once capacity is reached, with learners optionally placed on a waiting list. A learner cannot be enrolled in the same course twice concurrently, and course fees, where applicable, must be fully paid or a valid payment plan confirmed before access to paid course content is granted.

For self-paced courses, progress must be tracked based on the percentage of lessons or modules a learner has completed, and a course cannot be marked complete until all mandatory modules have been finished, regardless of optional modules. For instructor-led or live sessions, attendance must be recorded per session, and a minimum attendance threshold (for example, eighty percent of scheduled sessions) may be required before a learner becomes eligible to sit the final certification assessment. Progress and attendance data must be time-stamped and cannot be edited retroactively except by an administrator, with any such edit recorded in the audit log.

Where a course requires payment, the system must confirm successful payment through the integrated payment gateway before granting access to paid content, and must never grant access based on a pending or failed transaction. Refund eligibility must follow a defined policy, such as allowing a full refund only if requested within a specified number of days of purchase and before more than a small percentage of course content has been accessed. All financial transactions must be logged with a unique transaction reference, and any discrepancy between the payment gateway's record and the system's internal record must be flagged for administrative review rather than resolved automatically.

Every learner and instructor account must be associated with a unique identifier and a verified email address before the account is considered active. Learner records must retain a complete history of enrollments, assessment attempts, and certificates issued, and this history must not be deleted when a course is discontinued, since it may be needed for future verification of a previously earned certificate. Instructor records must capture the courses they are authorized to teach, and an instructor cannot grade an assessment or issue a certificate for a course they are not assigned to.

Access to the system must be governed strictly by the three defined roles — learner, instructor, and administrator — and a single account may not hold more than one role simultaneously unless explicitly granted by an administrator for a documented reason. New instructor and administrator accounts must be approved by an existing administrator before activation; self-registration is permitted only for the learner role. Any change to a user's role or permissions must be logged, and a user whose account has been suspended must be immediately prevented from logging in, without any residual access through an existing session.

Certification records, once issued, must be retained indefinitely or for a minimum period defined by institutional policy, since certificates may be verified by third parties years after issuance. The system must not permit the silent modification of an already-issued certificate; any correction must be handled by revoking the original and issuing a new, clearly versioned certificate, with both records retained and linked. All record-keeping must comply with the data protection and retention obligations described in Section 5.2, including the ability to produce an audit trail for any certificate upon request from an authorized party.

Core configuration values — such as passing marks, certificate validity periods, maximum quiz attempts, and grading scales — must be defined at the course level by an authorized instructor or administrator and must not be hard-coded into the application, so that different courses can operate under different rules without requiring code changes. Any change to a configuration value that affects an in-progress course (for example, altering the passing mark after learners have already started) must not be applied retroactively to attempts already completed under the previous configuration.

Certain actions must require a second-level approval before taking effect, including the manual override of an assessment result, the bulk issuance of certificates outside the normal automated workflow, and the deletion of a learner's academic record. Such actions must be initiated by one authorized user and approved by a second, distinct authorized user, following a maker-checker principle that prevents a single individual from unilaterally altering critical academic outcomes. Every approval decision, along with the identity of both the initiator and the approver and the timestamp of the action, must be permanently recorded in the audit log.

Together, the safety, security, quality, and business-rule requirements described in this section form the non-functional backbone of the Online Web-Based Training and Certification System. A learner-facing training platform succeeds not only by delivering course content correctly but by doing so safely, securely, reliably, and in a manner that upholds the trust placed in the certificates it issues. These requirements should be treated as binding constraints during design, development, and testing, and should be revisited whenever the system's scope, user base, or regulatory context changes.

Future revisions of this SRS should trace each functional feature back to the relevant requirements in this section, ensuring that, for example, every certificate-generation feature is checked against the audit and approval rules in Section 5.5, and every user-facing form is checked against the input validation requirements in Sections 5.2 and 5.3. This traceability is what allows the finished OWTCS to be evaluated objectively against the standards set out here, rather than against subjective impressions of quality.

An efficient and secure database is one of the most important components of the Online Web-Based Training and Certification System. The database stores all information related to users, administrators, courses, training videos, quizzes, certificates, and reports. A relational database management system such as MySQL is used because it provides high performance, reliability, data consistency, and security.

The database is designed using normalization techniques to minimize data redundancy and maintain data integrity. Each table is connected using primary keys and foreign keys to establish relationships among different entities. For example, a user can enroll in multiple courses, each course can contain multiple videos and quizzes, and every completed course can generate a certificate. These relationships ensure accurate data storage and retrieval.

The database also maintains records of user registrations, login history, course enrollments, quiz attempts, quiz results, certificate generation, and progress tracking. Backup and recovery mechanisms should be implemented to prevent data
loss. Appropriate indexing techniques should also be used to improve query performance and reduce response time.

In addition, the database should support concurrent access so that multiple users can use the system simultaneously without affecting performance. Data encryption techniques should be applied to protect sensitive user information such as passwords and personal details.

The Online Web-Based Training and Certification System must comply with all applicable legal and regulatory requirements related to software systems and online education platforms. The system should ensure that users' personal information is collected, processed, and stored according to privacy regulations.

The platform must protect users' confidential data by implementing secure authentication mechanisms and encrypted communication protocols. Passwords should never be stored in plain text; instead, they should be stored using secure hashing algorithms.

The system must also respect copyright laws. Training materials, videos, presentations, and learning resources uploaded by instructors should only be used with proper authorization. Unauthorized copying, downloading, or distribution of copyrighted content should be restricted.

Furthermore, digital certificates generated by the system should include unique identification numbers or QR codes to prevent forgery and enable certificate verification. The system should also comply with organizational policies and educational standards for online learning environments.

The Online Web-Based Training and Certification System is primarily designed for users within a single language environment. Therefore, internationalization is not included in the current version of the system. The platform will initially support the English language only, as it is the most commonly used language for educational content and online training.

Although internationalization is not required at this stage, the system architecture is designed in such a way that multilingual support can be added in future versions without major modifications. Future updates may include support for additional languages such as Urdu, Arabic, Chinese, and French to make the platform accessible to a wider audience.

The system also uses standard date formats, time formats, and Unicode character encoding to ensure compatibility with future language extensions. If the system is deployed internationally, localization features such as multiple currencies, regional date formats, and language translation can be integrated easily.

Since the current project is intended for local educational institutions and training organizations, implementing internationalization at this stage would increase development cost and complexity without providing significant benefits. Therefore, it has been marked as Not Required in the present version of the project.

The successful installation and deployment of the Online Web-Based Training and Certification System require both hardware and software resources. The system is designed as a web-based application and can be deployed on either a local server for testing or a cloud server for production use.

The recommended hardware includes an Intel Core i3 processor or above, at least 4 GB RAM, and 500 GB of available storage. A stable broadband internet connection is also necessary to ensure uninterrupted access to online courses, quizzes, and training videos.

On the software side, the system requires Windows 10 or Windows 11, a modern web browser such as Google Chrome, Mozilla Firefox, Microsoft Edge, or Safari, and a MySQL database server. During development, Visual Studio Code is used as the integrated development environment, while XAMPP or WAMP provides the Apache web server and MySQL database services.

The deployment process begins by installing the required software components, configuring the database, importing the project database, and updating the configuration files. After deployment, the administrator verifies database connectivity, user authentication, course access, and certificate generation to ensure that the system functions correctly.

For production deployment, SSL certificates should be installed to provide secure HTTPS communication. Regular backups, server monitoring, and software updates should also be implemented to maintain system reliability and security.

The Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC) is a structured methodology used to design, develop, test, deploy, and maintain software systems. It provides a systematic approach that helps developers produce high-quality software while meeting user requirements, maintaining project timelines, and ensuring cost-effectiveness.

For the Online Web-Based Training and Certification System, SDLC serves as the foundation of the entire development process. The project consists of multiple modules, including user registration, authentication, course management, learning content, quiz management, certificate generation, and administrative functions. Since these modules can be developed, tested, and improved independently, selecting the appropriate SDLC model is essential.

Several SDLC models are available, such as Waterfall, Agile, Spiral, Prototype, Incremental, and V-Model. Each model has its own strengths and is selected according to the project's nature and requirements. For this project, the Agile Model has been selected because it supports incremental development, continuous feedback, and flexibility in implementing improvements.

The Agile Model is a modern Software Development Life Cycle approach that focuses on developing software in small, manageable iterations called Sprints. Instead of completing the entire project at once, Agile divides the project into smaller modules. Each sprint includes planning, design, coding, testing, and review, resulting in a working part of the software.

For the Online Web-Based Training and Certification System, Agile is highly suitable because the system consists of several independent modules that can be developed separately. For example, the registration module can be completed first, followed by course management, quizzes, certificate generation, and reporting.

This approach allows developers to test each module individually, collect feedback, and make improvements before moving to the next sprint. As a result, software quality improves, development risks decrease, and user satisfaction increases.

Agile also encourages teamwork, continuous communication, and regular meetings among developers, testers, and stakeholders. This ensures that any issues or changes are identified early and resolved efficiently.

The Agile Model was selected because it provides greater flexibility and adaptability than traditional development models. Since web-based applications often require feature enhancements and user feedback during development, Agile supports continuous improvement without affecting the entire system.

The Online Web-Based Training and Certification System includes multiple independent modules such as login, course enrollment, quizzes, certificate generation, and reporting. Agile allows each of these modules to be developed and tested separately, reducing development complexity.

Another important reason for selecting Agile is that it promotes continuous testing. Bugs can be identified and corrected during every sprint rather than waiting until the end of the project. This significantly improves software quality and reduces maintenance costs.

Agile also encourages regular interaction with stakeholders. Feedback received after each sprint helps developers improve the system according to user expectations. This ensures that the final software meets both functional and non-functional requirements.
Furthermore, Agile improves project management because work is divided into short development cycles. Progress can be monitored more effectively, and project risks can be controlled at every stage.
Instead of following a strict sequential process, the Online Web-Based Training and Certification System was developed through multiple Agile sprints.

During the first sprint, project requirements were gathered, analyzed, and documented. Stakeholders identified the required features such as user registration, login, course management, quizzes, certificates, and reports. 8.5 Scenario: New User Registration, Course Enrollment, and Certificate Generation

A scenario describes the sequence of activities performed by a user while interacting with the system to accomplish a specific task. In the Online Web-Based Training and Certification System, one of the most common scenarios involves a new learner registering on the platform, enrolling in a training course, completing the learning activities, attempting quizzes, and finally receiving a certificate upon successful completion.

The process begins when a new user visits the system and selects the Registration option. The user enters personal information such as full name, email address, username, password, and other required details. The system validates the entered information to ensure that all mandatory fields are completed correctly and that the email address or username is not already registered. After successful validation, the user's account is created and stored securely in the database.

Once registered, the learner logs into the system using valid credentials. The system authenticates the user and redirects them to the learner dashboard, where all available training courses are displayed. The learner can browse different categories, read course descriptions, and select a course according to their interests or learning requirements.

After selecting a course, the learner completes the enrollment process. The system records the enrollment information and grants access to all learning materials associated with the selected course. These learning materials may include video lectures, PDF notes, presentations, assignments, and additional reading resources.

As the learner studies the course content, the system continuously tracks learning progress and stores completion records in the database. Once all learning modules have been completed, the learner becomes eligible to attempt the course quiz.

The learner starts the quiz, answers all questions within the specified time, and submits the responses. The system automatically evaluates the submitted answers and calculates the final score. If the learner achieves the minimum passing marks, the course is marked as successfully completed.

After successful completion of the course and quiz, the system automatically generates a digital certificate containing the learner's name, course title, completion date, certificate identification number, and verification details. The learner can preview, download, or print the certificate for future use.

If the learner fails to achieve the required passing score, the system checks the number of remaining quiz attempts. If additional attempts are available, the learner is allowed to retake the quiz. However, if the maximum number of permitted attempts has been reached, the system displays an appropriate notification informing the learner that no further attempts are allowed.
This scenario demonstrates the complete learning workflow of the Online Web-Based Training and Certification System, beginning with user registration and ending with successful certification.

A Sequence Diagram is a behavioral UML diagram that illustrates the chronological order of interactions between different system objects while performing a specific operation. It shows how messages are exchanged between users and system components over time, making it easier to understand the dynamic behavior of the software system.

In the Online Web-Based Training and Certification System, the Sequence Diagram represents the interaction between the Learner, Web Application, Database, Course Module, Quiz Module, and Certificate Module during the execution of a learning process. It clearly illustrates the sequence of requests and responses exchanged between these components.

The sequence begins when the learner submits login credentials. The web application forwards the login request to the database for authentication. After successful verification, the learner is granted access to the dashboard. The learner then selects and enrolls in a course. The enrollment request is processed by the application and stored in the database.

Next, the learner accesses the course content and completes all learning materials. Upon completion, the learner attempts the course quiz. The quiz module retrieves quiz questions from the database and presents them to the learner. After submission, the system evaluates the answers and calculates the obtained marks.

The application then checks whether the learner has achieved the required passing score. If the learner passes the assessment, the certificate generation module creates a digital certificate and stores the certificate information in the database. Finally, the certificate is displayed to the learner for downloading or printing.

If the learner fails the assessment, the system verifies the remaining quiz attempts. When attempts are available, the learner is allowed to retake the quiz. If no attempts remain, the system displays an appropriate message informing the learner that the maximum quiz attempt limit has been reached.

The Sequence Diagram helps developers understand the communication between different software modules, simplifies software implementation, and ensures that all interactions occur in the correct order. It also assists testers in verifying the execution flow and identifying possible communication errors between system components.

The objective of the testing phase is to verify that the Online Web-Based Training and Certification System (OWTCS) functions correctly according to the requirements defined in the Software Requirements Specification, and that it is reliable, secure, and usable for learners, instructors, and administrators. Since the system is a web-based application accessed by external users, all testing in this phase is performed using the Black Box Testing technique, in which the system is evaluated purely on the basis of its inputs and expected outputs, without reference to internal code structure.
Specific objectives of the testing phase are to:
Verify that all functional requirements (registration, login, enrollment, course content delivery, assessments, certification, and certificate generation) work as specified.
Validate non-functional requirements including performance, security, usability, compatibility, reliability, and scalability.
Identify, log, and track defects through to resolution.
Ensure traceability between requirements and executed test cases.
Obtain end-user (learner, instructor, and administrator) validation through User Acceptance Testing before deployment.
Testing is carried out at the following levels, all executed using black-box techniques:
Integration Testing: Verifies that combined modules (e.g., Enrollment ↔ Payment Gateway, Assessment ↔ Progress Tracking, Exam ↔ Certificate Generation) interact and exchange data correctly.
System Testing: Verifies the complete, integrated OWTCS against the full set of functional and non-functional requirements in an environment resembling production.
User Acceptance Testing (UAT): Performed by actual learners, instructors, and administrators to confirm the system meets real-world business needs before go-live.
Note: Unit testing (a white-box activity performed by developers on individual code components) is outside the scope of this document, which covers black-box testing only.
Testing was conducted in an environment that mirrors the intended production setup:
Application Server: Cloud-hosted server (Linux-based) running the OWTCS web application
Database Server: MySQL/PostgreSQL database server (staging instance with anonymized sample data)
Client Devices: Desktop (Windows 11, macOS), and mobile devices (Android, iOS)
Browsers: Google Chrome, Mozilla Firefox, Microsoft Edge, Safari (latest stable versions)
Network Conditions: Standard broadband and simulated 4G/mobile network for performance checks
Testing Tools: Selenium / manual black-box testing for functional cases; JMeter for load and performance testing; Postman for API-level black-box validation; OWASP ZAP for basic security scanning
Test Data: Dedicated staging database populated with sample learners, instructors, courses, and dummy payment sandbox credentials

Flow of the Online Web-Based Training and Certification System
The overall workflow of the system follows these steps:
– The student creates an account and logs into the system.
– The student views available courses and enrolls in the desired course.
– The student accesses study materials, including videos, documents, and presentations.
– The administrator creates quizzes, adds questions, and sets the passing criteria.
– The student attempts the online examination after completing the course.
– The system evaluates the submitted answers and calculates the score.
– If the student passes, the system generates a digital certificate with a unique certificate ID.
– The student downloads or prints the certificate, while the administrator can verify certificate records.
